I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over 40 years. My father farmed it before me, and his father before him. I know this soil and this weather. I don't need to think too hard about what to plant — everyone here plants winter wheat and summer maize. That rotation is what works on the North China Plain. The ground tells you what it wants.

My legs aren't as strong as they were, and my son is working in Handan city now, so I manage mostly alone with my wife. We have 8 mu. That's all I can handle. I will plant all 8 mu in wheat this coming October, then after harvest in June, I'll put maize in the same fields. I've done this every year since I was young.

For wheat, I'll buy improved seed from the village cooperative — the same variety I used last year, 矮抗58. It yields reliably and I know how it behaves. I'll use rotary tillage to prepare the bed, then apply compound fertilizer as base, then urea at jointing. I water three times: before winter, at jointing, and at heading. I spray herbicide in spring and a fungicide closer to harvest. That's my routine.

For maize, I'll direct-seed into the wheat stubble — no tillage, saves my back. I'll use a hybrid seed from the county seed shop. Maize doesn't need as much water if the rains come. I'll fertilize once at sowing and once at the big bell stage. Usually just one or two pesticide sprays, mainly for armyworm if it shows up.

I won't try anything new this year. New things bring risk and I'm 64. I need reliable income, not experiments.
